Title: Letter to Mr. Kiyoshi Tomizawa from Alfred H. Upham, 19 October 1937
Creator: Upham, Alfred H.
Summary: A letter from Alfred H. Upham, president of Miami University (1928-1945), to Mr. Kiyoshi Tomizawa, dated October 19, 1937. Upham discusses his family's plans for a winter vacation involving a trip around the world, with a potential stop in Japan. He expresses a desire to meet Tomizawa in San Francisco before their departure. Upham also reflects on Tomizawa's visit to Oxford in June, noting the warm friendships he reestablished and the pride in his work.
Transcript:
October 19, 1937

Mr. Kiyoshi Tomizawa
1528 Bush Street
San Francisco, California

My dear Tomizawa:

All summer and fall the Upham family have been
planning a winter vacation which would take the shape
of a trip around the world. In spite of many discourage-
ments we are still hopeful of carrying out our plans.
If we do, we shall sail from San Francisco at noon on
Saturday, November 13, using the President Hoover of
the Dollar Line. Of course these ships do not now touch
at any Chinese ports, but we are still hopeful that we
may be allowed to land at Yokohama and spend a number
of days in Japan. For that reason in particular I should
enjoy having opportunity for a chat with you either at
the pier or shortly before we sail. Since our time is
limited we do not expect to reach San Francisco before
Friday night. We shall probably stay overnight at the
Sir Francis Drake Hotel.

We all enjoyed your visit to Oxford in June quite
as much as I suspect you did. You reestablished many
warm friendships here, and we are all proud of the work
you are doing.

With all good wishes,

Very truly yours,

President

Title: Letter to the Minister from Siam regarding Prasob Sukhvashti, 20 October 1937
Creator: Upham, Alfred H.
Summary: A letter from Alfred H. Upham, president of Miami University (1928-1945), to the Minister from Siam at the Siamese Legation in Washington, D.C. The letter discusses Prasob Sukhvashti, a student who returned to Miami University to continue his studies. Upham praises Sukhvashti's academic performance and character, noting his determination and success in integrating into the university community. The letter supports Sukhvashti's plan to pursue a master's degree after completing his bachelor's degree.
Subject (FAST): correspondence; Miami University (Oxford, Ohio); international students
Transcript:
October 20, 1937

His Excellency, the Minister from Siam
Siamese Legation
Washington, D. C.

Dear Sir:

Prasob Sukhvashti, who has returned to Miami University
this fall to continue his college course here, has asked me
to write you regarding the record and impression he has made
on our campus.

During his earlier residence with us we all came to
think very highly of him, both on account of his natural
ability and because of the determination with which he went
to work to improve upon his record in the east and to
profit by the educational opportunities here. Except for
his wider experience he was just another Miami student, un-
assuming, dependable, and interested in what life here had
to offer. He did first class work in his studies and made
many friends among students and faculty. We have all been
delighted to have him return to us this year.

There is every indication that the young man has
entered upon his work this fall with the same fine spirit
he manifested before. In the interval he has had added ex-
perience in teaching and in newspaper work, so that he has
more definite objectives than before. His idea of continuing
here until he has completed work for the master's degree
seems to me entirely sound, since he will have slightly more
than enough credits for the A. B. degree at Commencement time
in June, and can qualify for the master's degree by the middle
of the next college year, about February 1, 1939. I am sure
that you may count upon him to do what he undertakes and ful-
fill all obligations.

Respectfully yours,

President

Title: Letter to President William M. Jardine from Alfred H. Upham, 20 October 1937
Creator: Upham, Alfred H.
Summary: A letter from Alfred H. Upham, president of Miami University (1928-1945), to President William M. Jardine of the University of Wichita. Upham discusses his plans for a sabbatical leave involving a trip around the world, with a scheduled departure from San Francisco on November 13. He seeks Jardine's advice and connections for the Cairo leg of his journey. Upham also mentions the public perception of university presidents taking sabbatical trips.
Transcript:
October 20, 1937

President William M. Jardine
University of Wichita
Wichita, Kansas

My dear Jardine:

You may recall that when I was in your home last
June I indicated with very little confidence that the
Uphams were hoping to utilize a sabbatical leave for
winter vacation this year for a trip around the world.
One obstacle after another seems to arise to prevent this,
but we are still pushing ahead with our plans and have en-
gaged passage on a boat leaving San Francisco November 13.
Of course we shall have to detour around China, and per-
haps a few other places, but we are due to reach Cairo
about February 14 and make that our headquarters until
the end of February. We have no detailed plans for those
two weeks but expect to make the trip to Luxor and also to
Jerusalem.

I am wondering if in the light of your experience
and acquaintance there you would have any suggestions you
would care to offer or would indicate any people whom we
ought to see. I am told that this is the busiest time of
the year there, and well understand how that would be so.
If only you and your family were located there once more,
this part of our trip would be a real holiday. As it is,
we shall be just some other American tourists.

I am not letting much publicity out in regard to
this winter trip, because however valuable it may be for
professors to enjoy sabbatical travel, the public hardly
approves of presidents doing such wasteful things.

With all good wishes,

Very truly yours,

President

Title: Letter to Mr. Koichi Hasegawa from the president, 19 October 1937
Creator: Upham, Alfred H.
Summary: A letter from Alfred H. Upham, president of Miami University (1928-1945), to Mr. Koichi Hasegawa in Osaka, Japan, dated 19 October 1937. Upham discusses his family's planned winter vacation, which includes a trip around the world with stops in Japan. He provides details of their itinerary, including stays in Yokohama, Tokyo, and Kyoto, and mentions arrangements made with American Express. Upham expresses hope that current conditions will not interfere with their plans and extends an invitation to meet Hasegawa during their visit.
Transcript:
October 19, 1937

Mr. Koichi Hasegawa
57 Naka 1 Chome
Sonezaki, Kitaku
Osaka, Japan

My dear Hasegawa:

In spite of many discouragements the Upham family is
still planning quite definitely a winter vacation which will
take the form of a trip around the world. We shall have to
be detoured around China, but we still have every assurance
that your country will be open to visitors and that we shall
have every opportunity to get around. I have heard from
Dr. Shideler, who has been in Japan until very recently and
who I believe saw you during his visit there. We would be
glad also to see you sometime and some place which proves
to be convenient for you during our all too limited stay in
the country.

Our present plan is to reach Yokohama on the President
Hoover on the morning of Saturday, November 27. We have
reservations at the Imperial Hotel in Tokyo for several days.
We are to reach Kioto Wednesday afternoon, December 1, and
will be at the Miyako Hotel there. We plan to sail from Kobe
Sunday, December 5. I am writing you these details so that
it may be easier for you to establish contact with us, and
not with the thought that you should feel any obligation what-
ever to show us around or do things for us. We have arranged
a rather busy itinerary with the American Express, and hope
that the rather unusual conditions now prevailing will not
interfere too seriously with what we should like to do.

With all good wishes,

Very truly yours,

President

Title: Foreword by A. H. Upham, undated
Creator: Upham, Alfred H.
Summary: This foreword by Alfred H. Upham, president of Miami University (1928-1945), introduces a book by Swasdi Nitibhom, a native of Thailand. The book is based on a ballroom dancing class conducted by Nitibhom for American students. Upham highlights the cultural exchange and the shared experiences between Thai students and their American counterparts at Miami University. He praises the grace and rhythm Nitibhom brings from his experiences in England and Thailand.
Subject (FAST): Miami University (Oxford, Ohio); international students; Thailand
Transcript:
[handwritten] Nitibhom

FOREWORD

Dancing, like music, is an art that has no boundaries
of race and language. This little book by a native of Thailand
has grown out of a voluntary class in ball-room dancing con-
ducted by him for a typical group of American students. He
perfected his art in England. His pupils have never witnessed
the subtle posturing of Siamese dancers or heard the temple-
bells that still echo in his ears. But they appreciate and
profit by the added grace and rhythm and sense of refined
beauty he has brought with him from other shores.

[handwritten] Swasdi Nitibhom and the little group of other young
men from Thailand who have chosen to live and work for a time
among us are very welcome here at Miami University. They have
sent our imaginations questing half way around the world. At
the same time, with their American nicknames, their interest
in our sports and recreations, and their ability to show us up
in the classroom, they have made us realize how much all stu-
dents everywhere have in common. We frankly admit that one of
them can effectively teach us to dance our own dances.

A. H. Upham

September 8, 1941

Mr. Murray Sheehan
Monsomhurst 59
Gloucaster, Massachusetts

Dear Murray:

Replying to your letter of September 6, I can
assure you that we shall be pleased to admit Karoom
Generdoomying to Miami University as a freshman.

While of course we know nothing of the University
you mention in Bangkok or of its entrance examinations,
the other boys from Thailand have made such a good

Freshman Week begins with a convocation next
Sunday evening, September 14, but we can hold a room
for him a little longer if necessary. We are trying
to squeeze him into one of the freshman dormitories.

Cordially yours,

President

Title: Letter to Mr. Murray Sheehan from the president, 19 November 1941
Creator: Upham, Alfred H.
Summary: A letter from Alfred H. Upham, president of Miami University (1928-1945), to Mr. Murray Sheehan at the Royal Thai Legation in Washington, D.C. Upham discusses the possibility of inviting a Thai minister to speak at the university's Commencement exercises in June 1942. He expresses concerns about potential diplomatic issues and his difficulty pronouncing Thai names. Upham also mentions the absence of some Thai students from the previous year and praises those currently at the university.
Subject (FAST): correspondence; Miami University (Oxford, Ohio); international students; Thailand
Transcript:
November 19, 1941

Mr. Murray Sheehan
Royal Thai Legation
2300 Kalorama Road
Washington, D. C.

Dear Murray:

I have just now got around to the problem of finding
speakers for our Commencement exercises next June. Naturally
I am greatly attracted by your suggestion that there is again
a minister from Thai in Washington who would qualify in every
way as our speaker on the regular Commencement program. I
have only two reservations which are quite obvious: one, that
for some reason or other this man also may be recalled before
our Commencement date; the other, that international friendships
in the Pacific area may crack all to pieces before that time
so that there may be no Thai minister in Washington at all.
However, I am willing to take chances on these contingencies.
There is a third difficulty in which I know you can help me.
That is, my utter inability to pronounce any of these Siamese
names correctly in public.

Seriously, I should be glad to have you extend our in-
vitation to the Minister to deliver the Commencement address
to the graduates of Miami University on the morning of Monday,
June 8, 1942, which is our regular Commencement date. If he
can arrange to undertake this responsibility, I shall hope of
course that you may find it convenient to escort him out here
and enjoy with him the Commencement atmosphere that always
characterizes Miami University.

I had hoped for an occasion which would take me to
Washington before this time. Unfortunately for me, the annual
meeting of the National Association of State Universities was
changed from Washington to Chicago because of the difficulty
of accommodating the Association in any Washington hotel.

We greatly miss some of our friends among the Thailand
boys who were with us last year. Those who are here at the
present time, however, are giving an excellent account of them-
selves.

With all good wishes,

Very truly yours,

President

June 2, 1942

President A. H. Upham

Oxford, Ohio

Dear President Upham:

Just a line, upon my return to the  
Legation, to thank you for the many courtesies which were

again how proud I am of the wonderful work which you are

Title: Letter to President A. H. Upham from C. V. Hibbard, 21 February 1944
Creator: Hibbard, C. V.
Summary: A letter from C. V. Hibbard, National Director of the National Japanese American Student Relocation Council, to Alfred H. Upham, president of Miami University. The letter discusses changes in the deferment policy for undergraduate students in scientific fields by the War Manpower Commission and the Selective Service System. It highlights the recommendation of Nisei students for deferment and includes a statement from Dean Everett L. Hunt of Swarthmore College supporting the deferment of Japanese-American students. Hibbard emphasizes the importance of considering Nisei students fairly in the quota lists.
Subject (FAST): correspondence; Miami University (Oxford, Ohio); Japanese Americans; World War (1939-1945); United States. Selective Service System
Transcript:
NATIONAL JAPANESE AMERICAN
STUDENT RELOCATION COUNCIL

1201 Chestnut Street, Philadelphia 7, Pa.
RITtenhouse 9372

John W. Nason, National Chairman                    C. V. Hibbard, National Director

February 21, 1944

President A. H. Upham
Miami University
Oxford, Ohio

Dear President Upham:

The War Manpower Commission in conjunction with the
Selective Service System has recently changed the basis for the
deferment of undergraduate students in Engineering, Physics,
Chemistry, and similar subjects. Each college or university
now has a quota assigned to it.

It has come to our attention that certain institutions
are recommending Nisei students for deferment in their quotas.
You may be interested in the statement of Dean Everett L. Hunt
of Swarthmore College.

"We are recommending our Japanese-American boys to
the National Roster of Scientific and Specialized
Personnel for deferment as engineers or chemists.
They have outstanding records and certainly deserve
this deferment. I am not sure that the western
draft boards will accept the recommendation of the
National Roster on this, as I understand they have
been ordered to reclassify all the 4-C boys.

"I want to assure you of our appreciation of the
excellent qualities of these boys, and of our in-
tention to do all we can to enable them to finish
their training under the same terms as are given
to outstanding scientific students of any other
race or group."

Nisei students should not, of course, be given prefer-
ential treatment. I do hope, however, that they will be given
consideration when you draw up the lists for your quotas.

Yours sincerely,

C. V. Hibbard, Director

Title: Letter regarding Wing Kong Chong, 24 April 1940
Creator: Lucas, Harold W.
Summary: A letter from Harold W. Lucas, General Secretary of the YMCA, to the President of Miami University, dated April 24, 1940. The letter provides a personal note regarding Wing Kong Chong, a student at Miami University who is expected to graduate in 1940. Lucas praises Chong's character and leadership qualities, expressing confidence in his potential as a teacher in Hawaii's Department of Public Instruction. Lucas has known Chong for eight years and speaks highly of his contributions during high school and summer camp.
Transcript:
[handwritten] Dear  
[handwritten] Miami University  
[handwritten] Oxford, Ohio  

OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT

MIAMI UNIVERSITY  
OXFORD, OHIO

April 24, 1940

President  
Miami University  
Oxford, Ohio

Dear Sir:

It has come to my attention that a personal note
from me might well be added to your file dealing with the
character and person of one of your students Wing Kong Chong
who, I understand, hopes to be graduated from your university
in 1940 with intention of returning to Hawaii to enter the
Department of Public Instruction as a teacher here. I am
very pleased to send this word of testimony concerning Mr.
Chong whom I have known for the past eight years. While I am
not qualified to speak for his scholastic ability or capacity
I do feel that I know enough of him and his brothers and sisters
to say definitely that he is the type of young man we are hoping
more and more will enter the public school system here.

I knew Wing Kong when he was in High School and during a
summer camp I came to know him even better. His character, I
believe, is above reproach. His willingness to be helpful and
his leadership even as a boy was very definitely an asset to
the camp. If, during his years on the mainland, he has contin-
ued on the path I knew him to follow, I am sure he will be a
splendid teacher and friend to youth.

Title: Financial assistance for Chinese students and trainees, 20 September 1945
Summary: A letter from the United States Department of State dated 20 September 1945, discussing financial assistance for Chinese students and trainees. The letter addresses the handling of visa applications for Chinese nationals proceeding to the United States for education. It emphasizes the need for colleges and universities to send notices of admittance directly to visa offices and to ensure that admittance is not conditional. The letter also highlights the importance of providing specific information about financial assistance to ensure its authenticity and adequacy.
Transcript:
[handwritten] F.13

ADDRESS OFFICIAL COMMUNICATIONS TO
THE SECRETARY OF STATE
WASHINGTON 25, D.C.

DEPARTMENT OF STATE
WASHINGTON

FOR VICTORY
BUY
UNITED
STATES
WAR
BONDS
AND
STAMPS

20 September 1945

Financial assistance given to students and trainees from China.
Admission of Chinese nationals to American colleges and universities.

The American Ambassador to China has made the following request
concerning the above two subjects:

"It would be helpful in the handling of the visa applications
of Chinese students and trainees proceeding to the United States if
the Department could make known as widely as possible to colleges
and universities, special bodies administering scholarship funds
such as the China Institute, and to American business organizations
accepting Chinese as trainees, that advice of the grant of scholar-
ships, fellowships, stipends and other financial assistance, should
be sent directly to the Embassy or to the consular office of the
district in which the applicant resides and that advice furnished
should be as specific as possible in regard to the amount of such
assistance. This is necessary in order to have some assurance of
the authenticity of the information and of the adequacy of the financial
assistance.

"It would be helpful if colleges and universities could be asked
to send their notices of admittance directly to the visa issuing
office and to make the admittance of students absolute and not condi-
tional upon the presentation of satisfactory credentials as frequently
is the case."

It should be noted that 4(e) visas may not be given when admis-
sion certificates are conditional.
